name: Makeupmaxxing

card.summary: Makeupmaxxing is the use of light cosmetics such as concealer, brow fill and bronzer to even out skin, define features and look better in person and on camera.
card.aka: makeup maxxing for men, male makeup
card.note: Products can trigger breakouts or irritation in some people; patch-testing and removal habits are part of the routine in community guides.

quick.overview:
Makeupmaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for men using cosmetics, usually subtly, to improve how their face reads. Typical goals are covering dark circles and blemishes, evening out skin tone, filling in sparse brows or beard areas, and adding light shading to bring out cheekbones and the jawline.

The payoff is immediate and reversible: the face looks clearer and more defined without any procedure. No clinical trials have studied makeupmaxxing as a looksmaxxing practice, so the evidence is mostly community guides and the general cosmetics literature on concealing and colouring.
quick.how: Community guides describe a layered, low-key approach: a concealer matched to skin tone for under-eyes and blemishes, brow pencil or gel to fill gaps, a bronzer or similar product to add warmth or subtle contour on the cheekbones and jaw, and sometimes lip balm or tint. Guides stress choosing shades close to natural skin so the result is 'almost non-noticeable'. Results are visible straight away and last until the products are removed.
quick.risks: Cosmetics can cause clogged pores, breakouts, or contact irritation in some users, and poorly matched shades can look obvious. Some forum members also describe social stigma as a drawback, which is why many guides recommend a subtle application. Makeup does not change underlying structure; it changes how light and colour fall on the face.

lead: Makeupmaxxing is a looksmaxxing term for using cosmetics, typically concealer, brow products and bronzer, to improve how a man's face looks. The goal is usually a more even complexion and clearer definition of features such as the brows, cheekbones and jaw, rather than an obviously made-up look.[1][3] Because it works on how light and colour fall on the face, the effect is immediate, lasts until the products are removed, and is fully reversible.

Looksmax.org guides present it as a fast, inexpensive, non-surgical route to a better appearance. One author describes it as 'the slight use of makeup' to look better every day and argues it can raise perceived attractiveness; another writes that the advice is meant to keep a masculine look while making changes 'almost-non-noticeable'.[1][3] Community members usually file it under softmaxxing, the non-invasive end of looksmaxxing that also includes skincare, grooming, clothing, weight management and exercise.[5]

Wikipedia's general cosmetics article notes that makeup has traditionally been used mainly by women, that men use it to enhance features or cover blemishes and dark circles, and that stigma around men wearing makeup in the United States has weakened while brands increasingly market to men.[4] Market-research figures reported by CNBC in January 2026 describe the shift: Statista data show the share of US men who never wear makeup falling from over 90% in 2019 to about 75% in 2024, and CNBC links makeup to a wider self-optimisation culture sometimes called looksmaxxing.[6]

chain: Concealer and tinted products even out skin tone and hide dark circles or blemishes
Brow fill and light shading add definition to the brows, cheekbones and jaw
A clearer, more defined face in person and in photos
angle.text: Makeup changes how the face looks while it is worn: concealer reduces the visibility of under-eye shadows and blemishes, brow products fill gaps, and bronzer or contour adds shading. Forum guides present it as the quickest adjustment available, with results the same day.

infobox: Concealer, brow pencil/gel, bronzer, lip balm

paras: Makeupmaxxing covers the use of everyday cosmetics by men to refine appearance. A guide on looksmax.org organises the topic by facial area: the cheekbone (zygomatic) region, under-eyes, acne and skin colour, lips, and the jawline, with a section on risks and side effects.[1]

A longer tutorial on the same forum describes escalating 'levels', beginning with the beard and eyebrow area and building toward fuller skin work, with the stated aim of staying subtle enough to read as natural.[3]

Wikipedia describes the main product types involved. Concealer is a cream or liquid, usually matched to skin tone, that is thicker and more pigmented than foundation and is used to cover marks and blemishes; variants include lighter eye concealers and colour-correcting concealers.[4] Bronzer is a powder, cream or liquid in matte, satin or shimmer finishes that gives a tanned look, and a bronzer brush can double as a contour brush; contouring is a technique for shaping an area of the face with shading.[4] Brow products such as pencils, creams, waxes, gels and powders colour, fill and define the brows, and brow tinting darkens the hairs without staining the skin beneath.[4]

The practices described in the forum guides each target a specific visible feature. Concealer is used on the under-eye area and on blemishes to reduce the visibility of dark circles and marks; brow fill closes gaps and adds shape; and bronzer or a similar shading product adds warmth or depth on the cheekbone and jaw.[1][3] The guides stress choosing shades close to natural skin tone so the result is 'almost-non-noticeable'.[3]

The retail products men reportedly buy in this category, according to CNBC, include concealer and concealer pens, tinted moisturisers and tinted SPF, brow gel, primer, setting powder and anti-shine powder.[6]

Looksmaxxing began in the 2010s on message boards and spread to TikTok in the early 2020s, according to Wikipedia's article on the term; that article does not itself discuss makeup.[5] Makeup advice appears on looksmax.org as threads framed as guides for men, including a multi-level tutorial and a guide organised by facial area.[1][3]

Outside the forums, mainstream business coverage places men's makeup in a longer trend. CNBC notes that CoverGirl named YouTuber James Charles its first 'CoverBoy' in 2016, and reports sales and survey figures: US men's grooming sales topped $7.1 billion in 2025 according to NielsenIQ, and Mintel found that 68% of Gen Z men aged 18 to 27 used facial skincare in 2024, up from 42% two years earlier.[6] An Ipsos figure in the same article puts US heterosexual men using cosmetics at about 15% in 2022, with another 17% saying they would consider it.[6]
The CNBC article names men's and gender-neutral brands such as War Paint, Stryx, TONE, Fenty Beauty and Unleashia, and quotes Sukoshi's CEO Linda Dang: 'This is no longer niche.'[6]

Forum posts frame makeup as an option that sits alongside skincare and grooming. One author writes that he expects people not to admit using makeup because it is seen as feminine, and argues that it can nonetheless improve a man's standing; he cites the influencer Clavicular as saying it is not a problem if it leads to better outcomes.[1] Wikipedia identifies Clavicular as the Kick livestreamer Braden Peters, profiled by The New York Times and The Guardian in February 2026.[5]

Another thread starter dismisses concerns that makeup is not masculine, arguing that such concerns can limit a person's options, while keeping the stated approach subtle.[3] A separate thread discusses a man with full-face powder makeup in Bangkok and the term 'gaymaxxing', showing that members disagree about how makeup is perceived.[2]

CNBC reports expert views that stigma is easing: FIT's Delphine Horvath is quoted saying that in ten years 'men's makeup' may no longer be discussed as a category, and Sukoshi's Linda Dang says the biggest barrier is uncertainty rather than price.[6]

The forum guide lists risks and side effects as a section of its own, reflecting that cosmetics can affect skin.[1] Wikipedia notes that fragrances, preservatives, emulsifiers and surfactants in cosmetics can trigger allergic contact dermatitis, and that fragrance can be listed under a single 'fragrance' label.[4] Heavy or occlusive products are also described as a possible contributor to perioral dermatitis, a rash around the mouth and nostrils.[7]

Poorly matched shades can look obvious, which is why guides recommend subtle application.[3] In the US, cosmetics generally need no FDA approval apart from colour additives, but manufacturers must ensure product safety, and the FDA can issue warning letters; the FD&C Act of 1938 gave the agency oversight of cosmetics.[4]
No studies found. Makeupmaxxing as a male looksmaxxing practice has not been the subject of published trials.

timeline.event: US Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act gives the FDA oversight of cosmetics.[4]
CoverGirl names James Charles its first 'CoverBoy'.[6]
More than 90% of US men said they never wear makeup (Statista, as reported by CNBC).[6]
Ipsos finds about 15% of US heterosexual men using cosmetics.[6]
About 75% of US men never wear makeup (Statista); 68% of Gen Z men use facial skincare (Mintel).[6]
US men's grooming sales top $7.1 billion (NielsenIQ).[6]
CNBC reports men's makeup going mainstream and tied to looksmaxxing culture.[6]

lore.intro: Makeupmaxxing is discussed on looksmax.org as a subtle, low-cost way to improve perceived looks, with debate over stigma and masculinity.[1][3]

claims.claim: Light makeup raises a man's attractiveness
claims.believers: Guide authors say makeup can increase a man's 'SMV' (sexual market value) and that it can make features such as cheekbones and under-eyes look better.[1]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested makeupmaxxing in men as a looksmaxxing practice.

claims.claim: Makeup can be applied so subtly that it keeps a masculine look
claims.believers: One tutorial author says the techniques are meant to go from non-noticeable to almost non-noticeable and to preserve a masculine look.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that stigma against men wearing makeup has weakened and that products are increasingly marketed to men.[4]

claims.claim: Makeup is not feminine and limiting yourself to 'masculine' norms is a handicap
claims.believers: The tutorial author calls 'alpha' and 'sigma' masculinity a major 'cope' and says non-binary-styled men can look better than most men.[3]
claims.experts: CNBC reports that Gen Z men are more comfortable with gender-neutral beauty and that retail experts expect the 'men's makeup' label to fade.[6]

claims.claim: Concealer and brow fill are the easiest, cheapest looksmaxxing adjustments
claims.believers: A guide author calls makeup 'easy, cheap' and effective and lists under-eye, blemish, lip and jaw uses.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes concealer and brow products as designed to cover marks and shape the brows.[4]

claims.claim: Cosmetics can cause breakouts or irritation
claims.believers: The forum guide includes a risks and side-effects section.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists fragrances and preservatives as causes of allergic contact dermatitis from cosmetics.[4]

claims.claim: Visible makeup draws attention or stigma, so it should be near-invisible
claims.believers: Members describe the aim as 'almost-non-noticeable'; a separate thread debates whether a heavy full-face look is 'gaymaxxing'.[2][3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and CNBC report that stigma has weakened in the US while some men still describe uncertainty about products.[4][6]
